notes.meaning: Abijah, the son of Rehoboam, became king while Jeroboam ruled the northern tribes. "Judah" here means the southern kingdom of Judah and Benjamin. The book of Kings says Abijah's heart was not fully right with God. This chapter adds the story of his great battle with Jeroboam.

Abijah ruled only three years. His mother is called Micaiah here and Maacah elsewhere. She was likely the granddaughter of Absalom, through her father Uriel. War soon broke out between Abijah and Jeroboam. No prophet stopped this war, because Jeroboam had turned from God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the writer mixed up Abijah's mother with Asa's mother, since both were called Maacah. Keil and Delitzsch reject this idea.

notes.meaning: Jeroboam's army was twice the size of Abijah's. He had ten tribes to draw from, while Abijah had only two. Even so, the smaller army would win. The battle does not always go to the strong.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Adam Clarke notes that many old Latin copies read 40,000, 80,000 and 50,000 slain. He thinks a zero may have been added by copyists. Keil and Delitzsch think the numbers mean that every fighting man in both kingdoms was called up.

notes.meaning: Before the fight, Abijah stood on a hill near Bethel and called out to Jeroboam's army. He was already inside enemy land. He tried reasoning with them before using force. It is wise to try fair words before reaching for the sword.

Abijah reminded them that God gave the throne to David's family forever. A "covenant of salt" means a lasting promise that cannot be broken. Salt keeps things from spoiling, and it was used with sacrifices. The Geneva Notes add that Abijah, not a godly man himself, used God's word to suit his own side.
Abijah called Jeroboam a servant who turned on his master. Solomon had once given Jeroboam a high post. Abijah left out that God himself had given Jeroboam the ten tribes because of Solomon's sins.

Abijah blamed worthless, wicked men for joining Jeroboam's revolt. He said Rehoboam was young, unsure and too weak to stand against them. In truth, Rehoboam was harsh and foolish at that meeting. Abijah was trying to make his father look as good as he could.
Fighting David's family meant fighting the kingdom of the LORD. Israel had a huge army and golden calves as gods. But those idols could not help them. They would bring God against them instead.

Jeroboam had driven out God's priests, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites. Instead, anyone who brought a young bull and seven rams could make himself a priest. Matthew Henry says fake priests suited fake gods well. The Geneva Notes say idol worshipers do not test the life or teaching of their ministers.
Abijah said Judah had not left the LORD. Their priests were the ones God chose, and the Levites did their work. Judah's faith had faults, but it was far better than Israel's idol worship.

Abijah listed the daily worship at the temple. There were burnt offerings and incense morning and evening, the holy bread on the table, and the lamps lit each night. All this was done just as God's law said. Wesley wonders if Abijah hoped this outward worship would make up for his own faults.

Abijah said God himself led Judah's army. The priests' trumpets were a sign of God's promise to remember his people in battle (Numbers 10:9). He warned Israel not to fight the God of their own fathers. It was foolish, and also ungrateful, to do so.

Jeroboam gave no answer to the speech. While Abijah was talking, he quietly sent troops around behind Judah. He trusted tricks and a big army, not the better cause. The Geneva Notes say he ignored good advice and hoped to win by deceit.

Judah suddenly found enemies in front and behind. In their danger they cried out to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets. No trap can cut off our way to God in prayer. God sometimes lets his people get into tight places to teach them to call on him.
The men of Judah shouted, and God struck Jeroboam's army. To the cry of prayer they added the shout of faith. The victory came from God, not from their own strength.
Israel's army ran away from Judah. God handed them over to Judah. Matthew Henry says God filled them with such fear that they could not fight back.

A huge number of Israel's soldiers were killed, more than half of Jeroboam's army. God was punishing Israel's idol worship. Yet it was sad that Israelites were killing Israelites. The bitterness of a civil war helps explain how fierce the slaughter was.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Adam Clarke thinks the number may first have been 50,000. He points to many old Latin copies that read it that way.

notes.meaning: Israel was brought low, and Judah won because they relied on the LORD. Relying means leaning on God's power and trusting him fully. The Geneva Notes say every kingdom's safety rests on trust in the Lord.

Abijah chased Jeroboam and took a few border towns, including Bethel. Bethel was where one of the golden calves stood. Matthew Henry wonders if Abijah left the calf standing, since his heart was not fully with God. He did not try to conquer all of Israel.

Jeroboam never got his strength back after this defeat. Later the LORD struck him and he died, about two years after Abijah. He escaped Abijah's sword, but no one escapes God's hand. Some think the blow was illness or grief, or the loss of his son foretold in 1 Kings 14.

Abijah grew strong and had a large family: fourteen wives and thirty-eight children. Since he reigned only three years, most of these marriages likely came over his whole life. His growing family was a sign of strength, while Jeroboam's family line soon ended.
More about Abijah was written by the prophet Iddo. That record is now lost. Matthew Henry notes Abijah's life was cut short soon after his victories.
